draftPackage.topic: Tesla Roadster: inverted surface grip and brief compressed-gas thrust
draftPackage.centralQuestion: How can surface suction and compressed-gas thrust produce two different surprising car maneuvers?
draftPackage.thesis: Understand pressure-difference surface grip versus gas-reaction thrust, and why brief airborne motion does not establish sustained practical flight.
draftPackage.viewerPayoff: Understand pressure-difference surface grip versus gas-reaction thrust, and why brief airborne motion does not establish sustained practical flight.

visualOpportunities.title: Stay attached, then push free
visualOpportunities.description: Large white wedge prototype on a curved ramp; separate brief hop. Clearly labeled illustrative reconstruction of reported events, not recovered footage or exact stunt trajectory. Match-cut same car from ramp contact to open space; visual accent separates suction/grip from gas thrust. Intimate side section: tire contact at surface and qualitative low-pressure space; animated evacuation outside body, no internal fan positions. Rotate whole view into inverted hold; sparse outside pressure arrows push toward surface; preserve contact and underfloor region. Hold inverted: gravity away from road and larger qualitative net pressure force toward it. No numeric vectors or calibrated relative scale. Camera pulls free of surface; explicitly attributed cold-gas principle, car free in open space. Enlarged detached principle inset shows gas release and opposite reaction, then applied qualitative motion with no visible proprietary nozzle hardware. Generic vectors next to car show translation, then off-center action changes orientation; no literal reconstruction of Tesla firing sequence. Separate abstract gas reservoir graphic progressively empties, detached from car body, not an internal tank design. Return to ramp/site motif and grounded car; two visual states recap contact grip versus brief thrust, ending lands rather than endless hover.

segments.text: Tesla showed a Roadster driving upside down, then briefly airborne.
But those are two different engineering tricks.
Tesla says fans remove air from beneath the car.
Lower pressure underneath lets outside air press it against the surface.
Upside down, that force must beat gravity.
Tesla attributes the airborne motion to cold-gas thrusters.
They release compressed air. Gas shoots one way; the car is pushed the other.
Different jet directions can change its motion. Off-center pushes can turn it.
But the stored gas is limited.
A short, controlled maneuver is not proof of sustained, practical flight.

misconceptionSafeguards: Suction needs a nearby contacting surface; it does not make airborne lift here.
Outside pressure presses toward the surface; gravity acts vertically down in the inverted view.
Gas release produces opposite reaction; rotation/translation distinct; schematic arrows not actual nozzle sites.
No dimensions, positions, architecture, gas mass/pressure, force, acceleration, range, production date, certification or endurance.
Exterior is an original approximation, every scene labeled reconstruction or physics illustration.
No proprietary footage, protected frames, logo, scraped sound or fake archival imagery.
Closing conclusion is evidence distinction, not a universal impossibility claim about flight.
review.comprehensionReview: Hook visibly contrasts contact and airborne states; same exterior carries identity; pressure and gas scenes each explain one causal step; finite storage and grounded ending close the flight distinction.
review.rightsReview: Only original procedural graphics and original audio; existing licensed fonts and Kokoro. News/site assets are research only. No licensing assumption needed for third-party footage.

careAssessment.rationale: General engineering education; no stunt instructions, pressure-vessel construction guidance, advertisement or practical flying-car certification claim.
